title: Runtime Policy Enforcement at the AI Agent-to-Tool Boundary
subtitle: Design and Validation of an Inline MCP/JSON-RPC Security Gateway

cards.label: pattern entries at historical test snapshot

contribution: MCP policy and inspection components return decisions and hash-chained audit evidence across supported integration paths; callers and transports have distinct enforcement responsibilities.
methods: Parse and validate JSON-RPC, including duplicate-key and malformed-input rejection.
Normalize potentially obfuscated content before inspection.
Evaluate server trust, capabilities, and content/policy signals.
Return allow/block decisions using path-specific enforcement semantics.
Record hash-chained audit evidence and SIEM-oriented telemetry.
evidence: Cited Python 3.12 CI: 723 passed, 81.91% statement coverage (5,644 statements, 1,021 missed); Python 3.10/3.11 jobs also succeeded.
The historical detector collection has 55 entries. A later dated inventory at c30075da1dc1d3fa7b843bb76be8e842fbfa6ae3 has 69 entries; these are inventory counts, not accuracy rates.
Cited job and source inventory: 21 core SIEM test functions and 7 scenario test functions, plus 9 Elastic rule records.
Reported development-set result for the later detector: 15/15 attack samples flagged and 3/15 benign flags. Not independently rerun here; not population precision/recall.
limitations: PolicyEngine provides tool/server and egress policies; stdio inspection applies detector/rate checks, not one universal five-stage gate.
HTTP inspection callers must honor returned decisions. Controls apply only to traffic through the implemented integration paths.
No production deployment, universal prevention, detector effectiveness or external pilot result is established.
reproduction: Install the documented development extras and run python -m pytest tests/ -q using the cited Linux CI configuration.
A different platform or dependency set may produce different counts/coverage. This poster is not a promise about the latest main.
